articles.title: Mail-voting crackdown moves ahead as Trump court win opens door to federal action
articles.summary: Gene Hamilton says federal agencies like USPS can now move forward with Trump's mail-in ballot safeguards after the Supreme Court's ruling.
articles.body: The next phase of President Donald Trump’s effort to change America’s mail-in-voting system is taking shape after the Supreme Court issued a largely favorable ruling for the White House in a challenge to Trump's mail-in ballot restrictions. Former White House deputy counsel Gene Hamilton said federal agencies such as the Postal Service can now move forward with parts of Trump’s election-integrity order, including new ballot-mail standards and efforts involving state citizenship lists, as opposing states wait to see which concrete federal actions could form the basis of new lawsuits. "It’s really interesting what the court did [and] it’s actually exactly what you would expect the court to do," Hamilton told Fox News Digital. TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN ON MAIL-IN VOTING RESTRICTIONS BEFORE MIDTERMS Hamilton said that when Trump directed USPS, DHS and DOJ to prepare for the new protocols, several states immediately claimed harm, but the court’s majority rejected their challenge. Originally, a Boston federal judge agreed with them, but the Supreme Court effectively said "you can’t enjoin [the feds] from thinking" — in Hamilton’s words — because no action had taken place yet. JACKSON RIPS INTO SUPREME COURT COLLEAGUES' 'SERIOUS LEGAL ERROR' ON TRUMP MAIL-IN VOTING ORDER "It reminds the American people … just because something might happen in the future [it] doesn't mean that you're actually harmed today, and that's really the crux of what the court did." Hamilton quipped that if the states challenging the order were proven right — and the possibility of future harm were enough to obtain a legal stay — his organization would "have a field day across the country" trying to head off new policies he and his clients oppose. In that regard, he added that the district judge ultimately overruled by the Supreme Court made an "egregious" misread of Article III powers and essentially said states can dictate which cases the attorney general and DOJ try to prosecute. He emphasized that the legal landscape could change quickly once Trump’s actions get underway, but said states challenging executive action must show a concrete or sufficiently imminent injury rather than rely on predictions about what agencies might eventually do. DHS APPROVES PLAN TO VERIFY VOTER CITIZENSHIP, MONITOR MAIL BALLOTS AS TRUMP PUSH INTENSIFIES Besides USPS, Trump’s order directs DHS to compile and provide states with lists of adult U.S. citizens, while DOJ was told to prioritize investigations and potential prosecutions involving ballots issued to ineligible voters. "Let’s see what the departments and agencies actually do. Well, let's see what they say they're going to do," Hamilton told Fox News Digital, as new concrete federal rules will come next. USPS WOULDN'T DELIVER BALLOTS IN STATES THAT REFUSE TO FORK OVER MAIL-IN VOTER INFO UNDER PROPOSED RULE The clock is ticking to implement the plan and respond to further legal challenges as states distribute mail ballots progressively earlier than in past decades. USPS first proposed its ballot-mail rule in June and has since finalized it, requiring standardized ballot envelopes and unique tracking barcodes while directing states to use a federal portal to identify voters receiving mailed federal ballots. States that fail to comply could see outbound federal ballot mail refused or returned. But the agency signaled at the time that it won’t implement the rule for the midterms unless the litigation is resolved. A separate injunction obtained in litigation by the League of Women Voters currently blocks USPS from implementing the rule. "Why wouldn't you take steps like getting a list of eligible voters, like asking the USPS to use standard mail security measures that they use for other things," Hamilton commented. Asked which provisions of Trump’s order the administration plans to implement following the ruling, when those actions would begin and how states would be directed to comply, the White House did not provide specifics. "These are commonsense measures that protect the security of mail-in ballots and ensure only Americans are electing American leaders. This administration will continue to lawfully enact the agenda President Trump was elected on — which includes the safety and security of our elections," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. California Attorney General Rob Bonta — who led the plaintiffs from 23 states along with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro — criticized the Supreme Court for letting Trump "try to make it harder for Americans to vote." Shapiro was listed separately because Pennsylvania Republican Attorney General David Sunday had not signed the state onto the suit. "Not so fast," the potential 2028 presidential candidate said in a statement. "Donald Trump does not run elections here in Pennsylvania — or in any state." "[The] SCOTUS decision does not deal with the substance of Trump’s unconstitutional Executive Order and does not mean his illegal attempt to restrict mail-in voting will go forward." On Wednesday, Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes responded to the ruling, declaring, "Over my dead body is that rule going to go into effect. We are going to fight this tooth and nail in the courts." Bonta pledged to continue the fight and noted that Obama-appointed Judge Indira Talwani of Boston had originally sided with the plaintiffs. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Hamilton predicted such disputes would produce another round of litigation as agencies make their next moves. "We have to get through the arbitrage of lower court proceedings, and I'm sure there's going to be a lot more fighting to come," he said. Shapiro echoed the plaintiffs’ opposition to the ruling, tweeting: "We’ll see the Trump Administration in court." Fox News Digital's Hannah Brennan and Melissa Chrise contributed to this report.

articles.title: Dems derided Trump’s midterm gamble — until he ended up winning big
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's mid-decade redistricting push netted Republicans at least 10 more right-leaning congressional seats ahead of the midterms.
articles.body: One year ago this week, Texas passed a new congressional redistricting map, giving President Donald Trump his first major victory in his push to give Republicans a big boost heading into the midterm elections by drawing more right-leaning districts. One year later, as they fight to hold their razor-thin House majority, Republicans are the big winners, with partisan redistricting netting them at least 10 additional right-leaning congressional seats in time for the midterms. Democrats and left-leaning pundits repeatedly railed against Trump's efforts and charged they would "shred our country’s democracy." Top Democrats aimed to fight fire with fire but fell short. Their efforts to keep pace with the GOP were derailed following major court rulings by the Supreme Court and Virginia's top court earlier this year, which were seen as major legal victories for Republicans. And the GOP scored another redistricting win earlier this month in Missouri, when a judge allowed a new map, backed by Trump and passed last year by Republican state lawmakers, to be used in November's elections. BLOCKBUSTER SUPREME COURT RULING IGNITES REDISTRICTING WARS ACROSS SOUTHERN STATES Progressive pundits that cast Trump’s push for Texas to redraw its congressional map before the 2026 midterms as a threat to voting rights and democracy. Among them was former MSNBC anchor Joy Reid. She branded the fight a "Voting Rights 911" and later titled a segment on "The Joy Reid Show" as "Texas’s War on Democracy Through Gerrymandering." John Oliver, host of "Last Week Tonight" on HBO, was also among a group of pundits that criticized the redistricting push as a power grab by Trump and the GOP. Oliver said gerrymandering was the practice of manipulating maps "to get the outcome you want," and called it "putting a heavy thumb on the scale of who gets elected." Fox News Digital reached out to representatives for Reid and Oliver to see if they continue to stand by their criticism, but didn't receive responses by the time this story was published. It wasn't just pundits who spoke out. Top Democrats also took action, after Trump, aiming to prevent what happened during his first term in the White House when Democrats reclaimed the House majority in the 2018 midterms, first floated the idea of rare, but not unheard of, mid-decade congressional redistricting. After Texas led the way last summer, Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin called a ruling by the conservative-dominated Supreme Court to greenlight the redistricting a victory for a "rigged map" meant to protect the GOP from midterm accountability. "But it will backfire," Martin predicted. California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led a successful redistricting effort in his Democrat-dominated state last year to negate the GOP gains in Texas, emphasized, "California will not sit idle as Trump and his Republican lapdogs shred our country’s democracy before our very eyes." TWIN COURT RULINGS RESHAPE HOUSE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS FIGHT UPHILL REDISTRICTING BATTLE And Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York, who considered but decided against redrawing congressional maps in the blue-leaning state, charged that Trump and Republicans were aiming to "erode our democracy and drag us toward authoritarianism." A veteran Republican strategist sees the Democrats' arguments as hypocritical. "The left’s overcharged political rhetoric is undermined by Governor Gavin Newsom’s willingness to spearhead a power grab in his state that eliminated at least 5 GOP congressional seats," Colin Reed told Fox News Digital. Reed argued that "Democratic leaders had the same goal as Republicans with mid-decade redistricting; they just weren’t as successful, but their intent makes any complaints about democracy ring hollow." But Democrats stand by their resistance. "Elected leaders in every state should respond aggressively to this unAmerican attempt to rig control of congress for a generation," John Bisognano, executive director of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, told Fox News Digital. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER While Texas and California were the first major battlegrounds in the redistricting war, the fight quickly spread from coast-to-coast. Republican-controlled Florida, Missouri, and Ohio and swing state North Carolina, where the GOP dominates the legislature, drew new maps as part of the president's push. But in blows to Republicans, a Utah district judge late last year rejected a congressional district map drawn by the state's GOP-dominated legislature and instead approved an alternate that created a Democratic-leaning district ahead of the midterms. And Republicans in Indiana's state Senate in December defied Trump, shooting down a redistricting bill that had passed the state House. But Democrats were dealt a major blow this spring when the Virginia Supreme Court struck down the Democrat-controlled state's congressional redistricting ballot measure, which would have produced up to four more left-leaning House seats. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Concurrently, a blockbuster decision by the U.S. Supreme Court that gutted key portions of the landmark Voting Rights Act – ruling that race should not dictate the redrawing of legislative districts – gave a handful of GOP-dominated Southern states the greenlight to move forward with redistricting. The legal rulings locked in an advantage for Republicans in this year's battle for the House. Now it's up to voters to decide which party will control Congress. But the redistricting fight is far from over. Democrat-controlled New York is taking steps toward redistricting in time for the 2028 elections. So is blue state Maryland, but a court ruling on Wednesday dealt Democrats a setback. A Maryland court blocked Democrats from adding a congressional redistricting initiative to the November ballot on Wednesday. The Democrat-backed effort would have allowed Maryland residents to vote on an amendment to the state constitution to let lawmakers redraw district maps ahead of the 2028 elections. Meanwhile, battleground Georgia, where Republicans currently control the governor's office and state legislature, is also mulling a move. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The gerrymandering crisis Trump started last year is is not over. We expect him to continue demanding new congressional maps that manipulate voting districts to protect Republicans despite what American voters want," Bisognano told Fox News Digital. He urged state leaders to speak out and draw "responsive maps to ensure the national congressional map reflects the make up and the will of the American people."

articles.title: Socialist mayoral candidate ignites online mockery for touting basic city service
articles.summary: Los Angeles councilmember Nithya Raman faces online mockery from the right after celebrating a supposed win that critics said led them to question if it was a parody.
articles.body: A Los Angeles councilwoman’s celebration of a newly painted neighborhood crosswalk has drawn online mockery after critics seized on the months-long timeline and glossy "street infrastructure" rollout for what they said amounted to a basic city service. Los Angeles Councilmember Nithya Raman, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, is facing online mockery after celebrating the completion of a neighborhood crosswalk project, which was first raised by the Los Feliz Neighborhood Council late last year, in a post on X. The post featured before-and-after images and thanked her field team for "continuing to problem-solve, push for solutions, and make our streets safer." "Dear Lord, Nithya. Your standards are so incredibly low," responded Richard Grenell, Presidential Envoy for Special Missions amid Donald Trump's second term. "They didn’t even fix the street, they painted over cracks. And it took them a year….." "Holy s—t, my sides...Nithya Raman's big accomplishment is taking 9 months to paint 7 yellow stripes over a cracked street?" quipped former L.A. mayoral candidate and reality television star Spencer Pratt. "How dumb do you have to be to post this? BAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHA" DEM'S MELTDOWN OVER ‘TERRORIST SYMPATHIZER’ HASAN PIKER TRIGGERS INSTANT CONSERVATIVE MOCKERY: ‘YIKES’ "This is beyond parody," responded conservative commentator Ben Shapiro. "Eight months to paint some yellow lines. Huge infrastructure victory! Make her mayor!" "They're calling it the most ambitious infrastructure project since the Golden Gate Bridge," added the Manhattan Institute's Chris Rufo. AOC'S SOCIALIST CREDENTIALS FACE FRESH SCRUTINY AFTER GLARING 7-YEAR GAP SURFACES: ‘VERY CONVENIENT’ Fox News Digital reached out to Raman’s office and Pratt for comment but did not receive a response before publication. Raman’s announcement labeled the work "Improving Our Neighborhood Street Infrastructure" and included before-and-after photos showing yellow crosswalk markings across the cracked roadway. She said the Los Feliz Neighborhood Council had brought the issue to her office in late 2025. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The post did not specify the project’s cost, when physical work began, which city department performed it or whether the work involved safety improvements beyond the painted markings.

articles.title: One of the world's hottest industries is sparking a blue-collar jobs boom
articles.summary: AI infrastructure spending is projected to drive U.S. industrial construction to $684 billion by 2031, creating massive demand for skilled trades workers.
articles.body: The race to build the infrastructure behind artificial intelligence is creating a new boom for America's blue-collar workforce, as construction firms scramble to fill jobs building data centers, power systems and the facilities that keep the technology running. The rapid buildout is putting a new premium on skilled trades, with data centers requiring armies of workers to prepare sites, pour concrete, install electrical systems and handle the infrastructure needed to bring them online. "For many years, there's been a lack of focus just in general from what is the benefit of a career in the trades," explained Cole Renken, general manager of Merlo America, the U.S. division of Italian construction equipment manufacturer Merlo Group. "It's a very stable income, very stable lifestyle that you can provide for," he added. ONE OF AMERICA'S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS SAYS AI IS CREATING JOBS — NOT REPLACING THEM Now, the AI infrastructure boom could bring renewed attention to those careers. U.S. construction spending is projected to climb from $2.22 trillion in 2026 to $2.85 trillion by 2031, according to a new report from Merlo America developed with predictive sales intelligence firm BiltData.ai. Industrial construction, which includes factories and data centers, is projected to reach $684 billion by 2031, representing 24% of total U.S. construction spending. Much of that growth is being driven by the infrastructure needed to power AI, cloud computing and 5G, with data centers emerging as a major source of construction and industrial activity. And building those facilities requires skilled workers at nearly every stage of a project. Renken said large projects require heavy-equipment operators to prepare sites and logistics workers to coordinate materials, followed by concrete workers, electricians, plumbers and other skilled trades as construction progresses. Electrical workers, he said, could face particularly high demand. A SOUTHERN STATE JUST TOOK THE TOP SPOT IN ONE OF THE WORLD’S FASTEST-GROWING INDUSTRIES And the jobs don't necessarily disappear once construction is complete. Brittany Kaiser, CEO of AI infrastructure company Alpha Compute, told Fox News Digital that data centers require workers not only to build the facilities and energy infrastructure, but also to install equipment, monitor operations, perform maintenance and support future expansion. "These are projects that can provide hundreds or thousands of jobs over many, many years," Kaiser said. "It's not a quick construction project." She described data centers as "a constant construction project," requiring workers across construction, electricity, energy development, monitoring and maintenance as facilities grow and expand. That ongoing demand could create opportunities for surrounding communities, particularly for workers who can be trained for specialized positions. "It's jobs that can also be taught and trained," Kaiser said. "So it's very possible to engage with the community on education and training initiatives to allow people to get access to these higher paying jobs that they didn't have a skill set for before." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But as projects multiply, finding enough skilled workers could become a challenge. Renken said shortages in the trades have persisted throughout much of his career and could intensify as more projects come online. The boom, he said, is also a reminder that even the most advanced technology depends on physical infrastructure and the skilled workers needed to build and maintain it. That need, he said, could bring new attention to skilled trades that have long been overshadowed by the focus on high-tech jobs. "To me, it has been kind of an overshadowed market that hasn't gotten the attention that it needs," he said.

articles.title: US judge repeats block on Trump’s bid to limit voting by mail
articles.summary: Order comes days before ballots go out for the midterms.
articles.body:
A United States federal judge has for a second time blocked the Trump administration’s overhaul of election rules aimed at limiting voting by mail.

District Judge Indira Talwani late on Thursday blocked the US Postal Service’s new ballot rules for 14 days, hours after the agency said they had taken effect .

The ruling is part of an ongoing battle prompted by President Donald Trump’s bid to limit voting by mail, which is heating up as the US heads towards midterm elections in November that will decide control of Congress and the Senate.

Nearly a third of American voters cast votes by mail. The first ballots for the midterms are due to be sent out in about a week.

The new rules require states to submit approved voter lists and follow new ballot formatting before USPS can deliver voting slips. The restrictions were enacted on Thursday after the Supreme Court cleared the way for them.

Talwani wrote in a statement late on Thursday that states “have neither time nor funds” to redesign ballots, update election systems or train officials on the new USPS portal before the upcoming election.

The fight traces back to March, when Trump ordered the Postal Service to withhold ballots unless states supplied approved voter lists and new formatting rules.

Voting rights groups and democratic officials sued, arguing only states and Congress, not the president, can set election rules. Talwani agreed, blocking the rules over the summer.

On Monday, the Supreme Court’s conservative majority threw out that earlier ruling on a technicality, saying that the legal challenge on which it was based was filed too early.

Democratic officials and voting rights groups quickly refiled their challenge once the rules became official, allowing Talwani to block them once more in a late-night order.

Separately, attorneys general from 24 states filed a new lawsuit this week making the same core argument: that only the Senate and Congress, not the president, can have constitutional authority to set election rules.

A hearing on the refiled case is scheduled for September 3, just as ballots are set to go out. That timeline means whatever Talwani or a higher court decides next could take effect as voting begins, or after it is already under way.

articles.title: Creatine actually works — which is exactly why you should read the fine print
articles.summary: The key fact: The creatine did something for people who were already training. The barbell is the intervention — the powder is just a rounding adjustment.
articles.body:
Most of my job is telling people that the numbers they hear on the news or on podcasts are misleading or not as important as they sound. Supplements are one of the easiest topics for this. Somebody gets excited about a compound, a study gets misquoted, and six months later there’s a $40 tub of it in every kitchen in America.

So it was a bit disorienting to sit down with the literature on creatine and find that the hype is actually attached to something real. Well, mostly real. Let me show you where the seams are.

Start with what creatine was actually invented to do. A meta-analysis out this year in Frontiers in Nutrition pooled eleven randomized trials of over-60s who lifted weights, half of them also taking creatine. The creatine group got stronger — significantly stronger, on average, than the people doing identical training without it.

Granted, the effect size of 0.31 sounds more impressive than it is until you translate it. An effect size of 0.31 means your average creatine-taker finished stronger than roughly 62 percent of the placebo group. Turn that around, and 38 out of every 100 people who took nothing still beat the average person in the study taking creatine. So that is a real edge, and I’d take it. It is also not what is being sold to you on Instagram today.

Now here’s the study that should make you distrust your own bathroom scale: A team at the University of New South Wales published a trial last year in Nutrients . They supervised 63 adults — half on five grams of creatine a day and half on placebo — through 12 weeks of supervised lifting. However, they also built in a seven-day “wash-in” before anybody touched a weight, and they scanned everyone with DEXA at every stage.

After that first week of creatine and precisely zero exercise, the supplement group had put on half a kilo of what the scanner read as “lean body mass.” But muscle doesn’t materialize in seven days. Rather, that was just water being pulled into muscle cells, which the DEXA scanner obligingly counts as lean tissue. Then, over the 12 weeks of actual training that followed, both groups put on about two kilos, and the gap between them went away — same training, same result whether or not you were paying for the powder.

I keep coming back to that study because of what it explains. Everyone who has ever started creatine, weighed themselves five days later and felt enormous was not making it up. They measured a real thing at the wrong moment and drew the wrong conclusion from it. What I would like you to consider is that the industry has been quietly selling that first week for 30 years. The instrument and the customer are both fooled, even though the whole thing is sincere enough that nobody involved is lying about anything.

Then there’s the brain business. Sometime around 2024, creatine started being marketed as a cognition- and memory-enhancing substance rather than a gym aid. One industry analysis counted 469 podcast episodes on creatine in 2025 alone — more than the entire preceding decade put together — with brain-focused framing in the titles nearly doubling in two years and one title in six telling the listener she needs to be taking this.

The evidence underneath all that noise is thin. A 2024 review pooled sixteen randomized trials on creatine and cognition. The total number of participants in all of these was only 492 people, spread across ages 20 to 76, on different doses, for different durations, tested on different instruments. The review found small improvements in memory and attention and no statistically significant effect on overall cognitive function or executive function.

And there is a recurring statistical problem in this corner of the literature that I think deserves naming. When an earlier meta-analysis in Nutrition Reviews reported a memory benefit, a letter to the same journal pointed out that several outcomes measured on the same participants had been treated as if they were independent observations — in other words, they were double-counting the benefits. This narrows the confidence interval artificially and makes a wobbly result look settled. It is a boring, technical error, but it makes a difference and it is everywhere.

Break those same memory results out by age, and the story falls apart entirely. For adults 66 to 76, the effect size is genuinely large, but the effect is negligible for ages 11 to 31. So a fair reading would be that creatine might do something for an older brain running short on metabolic headroom, but it does approximately nothing measurable for a well-rested 27 year-old — you know, the guy who is actually buying all that creatine.

In fairness, I should also point out that the panic over safety of creatine has badly outrun the data. Creatine does not hurt healthy kidneys. The International Society of Sports Nutrition says so. A meta-analysis of renal function in athletes says so. And a full season of monitoring in 71 female soccer players turned up nothing beyond clinically trivial wobble in the bloodwork.

Creatine does raise serum creatinine (note the extra two letters in the spelling), which happens to be the metabolite your doctor uses as a proxy for kidney function. So your lab report might look frightening after you take creatine, even if nothing is actually wrong with your kidneys. If you have kidney disease already, ask your doctor before taking creatine. If you haven’t, then tell him you are taking it before he tests you and panics over your labs.

I want to finish with the study that keeps me cautious, even as I’m being persuaded. The biggest and longest trial in the field put 237 postmenopausal women on about 10 grams a day for two years, alongside supervised resistance training and walking. The primary endpoint was femoral neck bone density. The result was null — no effect on bone, bench press or hack squat. Creatine did produce a faster 80-metre walk, about a second and a half, and that finding is solid.

The lean tissue gain you will see quoted everywhere came out of a sub-analysis of valid completers rather than the randomized sample, and only 174 of the 237 women finished. So that is, at best, encouraging and inconclusive. But that is not how you will see it described on a label.

Five grams a day of creatine monohydrate is cheap, better studied than nearly anything else on the supplement shelf, and possibly useful for some people. If you are over 60 and lifting weights, then I think it is not a terrible idea, and I’d say the same to my own mother.

But look at what every single one of those findings has in common: The creatine did something for people who were already training. The barbell is the intervention — the powder is just a rounding adjustment.

So buy it if you want, but remember that it’s the weight-lifting that’s important, not the supplement.

Dr. Liberty Vittert Capito is a professor of the practice of data science at Washington University in St. Louis.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Bad Bunny, Marxism and 'Nasty Women' among courses offered at Ivy League, elite colleges
articles.summary: From Bad Bunny courses at Princeton and Yale to "Decolonizing French Food" at Penn, elite universities offer classes YAF report calls indoctrination.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: From "Religion and Nasty Women" to "Decolonizing French Food," students at some of America’s most prestigious universities can take courses on Bad Bunny, Marxism, gender and even why dancing matters if the world is ending. Collegiate conservative organization Young America’s Foundation (YAF) shared the eye-catching offerings in its 2026-27 "Comedy & Tragedy Report," obtained exclusively by Fox News Digital. At Columbia University, "Religion and Nasty Women" takes its name in part from President Donald Trump’s "nasty woman" remark about Hillary Clinton during the 2016 presidential campaign. CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM EXTENDS BEYOND STUDENT PROTESTS AND INTO CLASSROOMS, ADL WARNS The course description says the phrase has since become a "badge of honor and a rallying cry for women’s empowerment." Students examine goddesses, prostitutes and virgins across several religious traditions in what the description calls a survey of "religious-based misogyny" and women’s responses to it. Columbia also offers "Marxism and Cultural Theory," though the course description makes clear students shouldn’t expect a deep dive into Marx himself. LIZ PEEK: TRUMP IS STARVING THE MACHINE THAT CREATES AMERICA'S SOCIALIST REVOLUTIONARIES "This course will not offer an intensive study of the writings of Karl Marx," the description states. Instead, the class examines Marxism as a theory of culture, including its relationship to global capitalism, financial crises and other "discourses of social justice." Bad Bunny, aka Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio, may need to add college course namesake to his list of accomplishments, with the Puerto Rican musician suddenly inspiring multiple classes at elite universities. CONFIDENCE IN HIGHER EDUCATION SLIPS AFTER BRIEF RECOVERY, GALLUP POLL FINDS At Princeton, "Thinking with Bad Bunny: the Cultural Politics of Race, Language, and Empire" examines his music, lyrics, activism, "gender non-conforming performances" and business strategies. The course also explores how Bad Bunny navigates his status as a global Latino icon, while coming from what its description calls "Puerto Rico's colonial context." THE PROGRESSIVE EDUCATION MACHINE IS COLLAPSING. WE SHOULD LET IT FALL Yale gets in on the Bad Bunny action, too, with "Bad Bunny: Musical Aesthetics and Politics," a course examining his music alongside Puerto Rico's history, politics and "colonial past and present." At the University of Pennsylvania, "Decolonizing French Food" starts with wine, cheese and baguettes before examining how French culinary traditions have been shaped by colonialism. Stanford University’s "Gender in the Wild" course reportedly examines how gender shapes ideas about wilderness, freedom, heroism and risk, drawing on feminist texts, "Indigenous knowledge" and "Black environmental thought." DEMOCRATS OUTNUMBER REPUBLICANS 6-TO-1 AMONG COLLEGE GRADUATION SPEAKERS, REPORT FINDS Swarthmore College offers "Queering God: Feminist and Queer Theology," a religion course examining feminist and queer interpretations of God. "The God of the Bible and later Jewish and Christian literature is distinctively masculine, definitely male. Or is He?" the course description asks. The class explores whether characteristics including nurturing, forgiveness and love can be understood as feminine or female, and seeks to "stretch the limits of gendering-and sexing-the divine." Swarthmore also offers "The Fat Renaissance," which examines depictions of body size in early modern England and their relationship to what the course description calls the modern-day "obsession with bodily regulation and control of body size." The class is taught from the perspective of "conscious respect for bodily diversity." For YAF, the unusual subjects are no laughing matter. MED SCHOOL DEANS COME UP EMPTY IN TENSE HEARING WHEN ASKED POINT BLANK IF MEN CAN HAVE BABIES: 'RIDICULOUS' "Higher education has been hijacked by progressive ideology, transforming too many of our colleges and universities from places of learning into institutions of indoctrination," YAF President Gov. Scott Walker said. "This report pulls back the curtain on what students are being taught and exposes just how deeply ideological agendas have taken root on campus. "That is why YAF is fighting back, to ensure students receive an education, not an indoctrination, and to restore intellectual freedom and academic excellence to America’s campuses." The courses reported also come with elite-school price tags. YAF estimates a three-credit course at Princeton costs $5,778, while its report puts the equivalent at $5,613 at Penn. The organization says its estimates are based on U.S. Department of Education tuition data, with annual tuition at flat-rate institutions divided by a standard 30-credit academic year. YAF told Fox News Digital it surveyed available course catalogs covering the 2026-27 academic year from schools in the Ivy League, Big Ten, SEC and PAC-12, along with U.S. News & World Report’s top 10 liberal arts colleges. The organization said course titles and descriptions were reproduced unedited from university websites and course catalogs, and said its selections represent a sample rather than an exhaustive list. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP YAF has published its "Comedy & Tragedy Report" since 1995, arguing that the courses it documents demonstrate a lack of ideological diversity in higher education.Columbia, Princeton, Penn, Stanford and Yale did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

articles.title: Iran war shifts into neutral as 6-month mark arrives
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Iran war approach shifts ▪ Trump gives Paxton a boost ▪ Warsh makes key Fed speech ▪ Leavitt’s last day Today marks six months since the start of the war with Iran, which President Trump said would last for four to five weeks. The conflict has settled into a tense but relatively quiet holding…
articles.body:
Today marks six months since the start of the war with Iran, which President Trump said would last for four to five weeks.

The conflict has settled into a tense but relatively quiet holding pattern, as the Trump administration pivots into an economic pressure campaign weeks ahead of midterm elections, assuring Americans that negotiations are playing out behind the scenes.

With few public details emerging about the “economic D-Day” that Trump pledged to unleash on Iran, the unpopular war has taken a back seat to other news — at least for the moment.

The Trump administration seems to be content with the status quo in the Strait of Hormuz, despite occasional attacks from Iran.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said Thursday an oil tanker was hit in the Strait of Hormuz, but the crew was safe and no environmental damage was reported.

Gas prices, while still high, have largely stabilized at just above an average of $4 a gallon.

Oil is also passing through the strait — even though levels are well below what they were six months ago. According to Lloyd’s List Intelligence, last week’s ship traffic was up 50 percent from the week before.

The government has said 9 million barrels are passing through the strait each day — still shy of the roughly 15 million barrels that passed through before the war — while some analysts suggest the number is closer to 2 million to 6 million barrels each day, The Associated Press reported.

U.S. Central Command said Thursday that it had cleared all Iranian sea mines from the strait, freeing internationally recognized trade routes.

Trump, meanwhile, has shifted attention to a trade war with Canada, which carries its own political risks for Republicans, particularly in some key battleground states along the border .

After trade negotiations fell apart a week ago, a 50 percent tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports took effect. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by announcing “dollar for dollar” retaliatory tariffs, starting Sept. 8.

Trump on Thursday summoned reporters to the Oval Office for the signing an executive order changing Lake Ontario’s name to “Lake America” — a provocation that garnered blowback from many Democratic officials and Canadian leaders.

When a reporter asked Trump about the latest developments in the economic pressure campaign against Iran, the president said, “There’s not a lot to speak to,” and suggested the U.S. has the situation under control in the Strait of Hormuz.

“The strait is open. We’re taking a lot of boats. Millions and millions of barrels of oil are coming out of the strait every day. Other countries recognize that,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office yesterday, adding, “We’ve totally cleared the strait of mines.”

“But we’re watching,” the president said. “ We see every inch of the strait, and any boat [that] goes in with a mine, we see it, and we take it out.”

Some analysts warn that the situation can change at any moment. The run-up to the midterms provides Iran a unique opportunity to leverage Americans’ reluctance to reengage in open conflict, making the moment especially precarious.

“While the conflict with Iran appears to have cooled somewhat over the past week, with the focus shifting toward economic sanctions, the situation remains highly volatile. Military action by either side could quickly change the trajectory of the conflict ,” GOP strategist Ron Bonjean told Morning Report.

“As long as the war continues to keep gas prices elevated, it remains a political vulnerability for Republicans heading into the elections,” he continued. “ Voters feel high prices at the pump immediately and that keeps the issue front and center.”

Republican strategist Bill O’Reilly similarly said what matters most is gas prices leading up to Election Day.

“The price of gas and oil in late October could be make or break in this election. Actions that ensure predictable oil flow will help Republicans,” O’Reilly said. “Events that continue the disruptions would pose additional challenges to the GOP.”

▪ The Hill : Canada excludes seafood from retaliatory tariffs.

▪ The Guardian : War rapidly draining U.S. Navy budget.

▪ Reuters : Iran war has reached its endgame — a costly stalemate.

The back and forth between Trump and Carney isn’t slowing down. The president announced the renaming of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” as he’s also threatening 50 percent auto tariffs starting next year. I spoke with Peter Navarro , the senior counselor to the president for trade and manufacturing, and he noted one thing in particular said by the president.

“We gave them a beautiful deal. That deal was well worth signing, and they didn’t do it. The president is disappointed,” Navarro told me . “And that’s the worst word you can hear from President Donald J. Trump.”

There are 127 days left in the year, leaving time for this relationship to potentially patch back together before the president’s deadline. However, as we’ve often seen with tariffs, those deadlines can move at any time.

Burman hosts “The Hill” weeknights, 6 p.m. EDT/5 p.m. CDT on NewsNation.

A federal judge has again blocked the Trump administration from going forward with its new mail-in voting restrictions from the president’s executive order, pausing the move for at least two weeks . That would extend beyond when the first states start sending out mail-in ballots for the midterms.

Three employees of Stars and Stripes sued the Pentagon over their firings, alleging their removals last week violate the department’s own personnel rules and the First Amendment. The lawsuit is the latest development in the ongoing battle over the outlet’s independence from the Defense Department.

A federal judge in California ruled that the Pentagon’s blacklisting of the AI firm Anthropic earlier this year was illegal as it violated the First and Fifth amendments . The company has also sued over the administration’s actions in Washington, D.C.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican candidate for the U.S. Senate, waves as he takes the stage during a primary runoff election night event after winning the Republican party’s nomination, May 26, 2026, in Plano, Texas. (Tony Gutierrez, Associated Press)

CHOOSING TEXAS : The president traveled to the Lone Star State on Thursday in an effort to boost the Senate candidacy of state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) as the race becomes one of the most hotly contested in the country.

Democrats have been feeling increasingly hopeful about their chances of flipping Texas blue with state Rep. James Talarico opposing Paxton for Sen. John Cornyn ’s (R) seat. A Texas Public Opinion Research poll released Thursday found Talarico ahead of Paxton by 7 points, while election handicapper Cook Political Report shifted its rating of the race from “lean Republican” to “toss up” last week.

The Hill’s Julia Manchester reports Texas has been taking up more oxygen in the GOP’s push to keep hold of the Senate majority, raising questions as to whether Republican spending in Texas is taking focus away from other critical races.

The ad-tracking firm AdImpact predicted in June that a whopping $446 million would be spent on political ads in the state, a striking increase from its original projection of $124 million.

“A competitive Texas is a very expensive date for us,” said Dan Eberhart , a Republican donor who is supporting Paxton.

articles.title: Who’s to blame for sky-high energy bills in New York? Not Trump.
articles.summary: Elected officials everywhere are under pressure to bring prices down; dumping costly climate laws that outlaw the use of abundant and relatively cheap fossil fuels is an attractive fix.
articles.body:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) recently attacked President Trump for driving up energy prices for New Yorkers. She warned that Trump’s trade dispute with Canada could lead to higher costs for New York residents after Ontario Premier Doug Ford threatened to retaliate by cutting electricity exports to the U.S.

“There’s exactly one person to blame when electricity bills go up: Donald Trump,” Hochul said .

One might wonder why New Yorkers depend on Canada to supply their electricity when the U.S. is the world’s biggest oil producer , and our country’s natural gas output, the largest feedstock for electricity production, has expanded by nearly 50 percent over the past decade.

As the New York governor well knows, it is the war waged by herself and her predecessor, Andrew Cuomo (D), against those same fossil fuels (which supply some 60 percent of the nation’s electricity) that have spiked electricity prices in her state. Also boosting costs was the former governor’s boneheaded decision to shut down the Indian Point nuclear power station . Those two disastrous policies combined to push residential electricity prices in New York fully 62 percent above the national average, the third highest in the nation . Cuomo and Hochul traded affordable electricity for votes and donations from climate zealots, in the process costing residents of the Empire State billions of dollars.

Yes, oil prices have climbed 25 percent over the past year, in large part because of the war with Iran. But that jump pales in significance to what New York did by formally banning fracking in 2015, thus depriving residents not only of jobs and income but also plentiful natural gas. It is no surprise that electricity prices in Pennsylvania, which allowed fracking of the Marcellus shale in their state, are about 30 percent lower than in Hochul’s New York.

We know the Cuomo-Hochul assault on fossil fuels is damaging New York because the current administration has moved to postpone some of the draconian requirements of the state’s climate laws. New York’s 2019 Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act , one of the strictest in the nation, was supposed to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 40 percent compared to 1990 levels, and by 85 percent by 2050. It also required the state to transition to 100 percent zero-emission electricity by 2040 .

Integral to the bill was a cap-and-trade program that Hochul argued in a memo would impose costs of more than $4,000 annually per family in 2031. Politico has since called Hochul’s waffling on this issue “one of the clearest signs yet that Democrats are recalibrating their climate agenda as the party increasingly prioritizes affordability ahead of the midterms.”

But even Hochul cannot fool all of the people all of the time. New York State residents, concerned about affordability, will no longer accept her preposterous kowtowing to the radical climate activists clamoring, apparently, to eat by candlelight in unheated homes.

Of course, New York is not the only Democrat-run state sacrificing its citizens on the altar of climate change. Blue states in general have higher energy costs than red states, according to data compiled by researcher Sarah Montalbano and published by the Institute for Energy Research.

They found that the divergence has grown larger and larger. As of 2011, blue-state electricity rates were on average of 44 percent higher than in red states. By 2025, blue state rates had risen much faster and were 61 percent higher than in red states.

The study indicates that the growing gap between blue and red states’ electricity prices is driven by policy choices. If regional or geographic factors were to blame, the cost difference would likely remain constant.

The group details especially what it calls the “explosion in electricity prices in some of the country’s most notorious blue-state policy regions, such as New England and California,” noting that the Golden State “has become a poster child for the ballooning costs of an electric grid that is increasingly reliant on wind, solar, and battery storage.” New England, for its part, has taken the lead in shunning abundant and relatively clean natural gas.

The penalty for living in climate-obsessed California or New England is severe. Since 2011, the data show , electricity prices in those two regions have soared nearly four times faster than the other 42 states. Specifically, electricity rates in California and New England have jumped by 90 percent, compared to just 23 percent in the rest of the country.

New York was not the first high-cost energy state to walk back deleterious climate legislation. Connecticut earned that distinction in June 2025, when it took the lead in rescinding an onerous renewable energy mandate. The state reduced its renewable energy target from 40 percent to 29 percent for 2030, and from 32 percent to 25 percent for 2026. The changes are expected to save somewhere around $60 million per year starting in 2026, lowering residential electric bills by around 14 percent.

All across the country, and indeed all across the developed world, policymakers are reassessing the costs of climate policies. Trump led the charge, dismantling much of former President Joe Biden’s green initiatives, much to the disgust of European leaders who have been in the vanguard of erecting costly climate hurdles that have slowed their growth and crippled their industries.

As The Wall Street Journal recently reported , “The European Union has proposed to relax its landmark carbon-pricing system” and pushing back its deadline for the elimination of internal combustion car sales. The U.K. is also considering pursuing reopening North Sea acreage to new oil exploration and may dump its support for elective vehicles. Canada, meanwhile, is abandoning what the Journal called “an unpopular carbon tax” and continues to develop new infrastructure for its thriving oil and gas industries.

Elected officials everywhere are under pressure to bring prices down; dumping costly climate laws that outlaw the use of abundant and relatively cheap fossil fuels is an attractive fix.

Liz Peek is a former partner of major bracket Wall Street firm Wertheim and Company.

articles.title: Whole Hog Politics: Trump finds an easier midterm foe in his own party
articles.summary: [Watch Whole Hog Politics live: Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. ET as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon break down this week’s political news and answer questions from a live online audience.] There is a rhythm like the seasons to a midterm election year. First, when there’s still frost…
articles.body:
[ Watch Whole Hog Politics live : Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. ET as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon break down this week’s political news and answer questions from a live online audience. ]

There is a rhythm like the seasons to a midterm election year.

First, when there’s still frost on the ground, members of the party in power explain how this year, akshually , they’re not going to lose.

Then come the torrents of spring, bringing panic and despair as it becomes clear they akshually will.

Then follows the summer heat of irrational exuberance from the party out of power.

Then, as fall approaches and primaries pass, party unity is restored and the true landscape is revealed.

Then comes the cold November rain: reversal, defeat and disappointment.

But after all that, there’s always a coda: bitter recriminations gusting in like winter wind under a drafty door. Lawmakers in the losing party quietly — or sometimes not so quietly — blame the president’s policies. And presidents — to their own varying degrees of bluntness — put the blame back on the lawmakers for failing to fully embrace their agenda.

During his presidency, Barack Obama and his team had a couple of opportunities to blame Democrats: the stinging rebukes of 2010 and 2014. In both cases, but particularly in the former, the message was that “purist” Democrats had abandoned the party in midterms because they were unwilling to accept compromises. The policies, most notably ObamaCare, weren’t the problem, he said, but rather “sanctimonious” progressives who didn’t know a good thing when they saw it.

That was very much like what the Clinton administration did after the thumping 1994 loss in Bill Clinton ’s first term. Through strategic leaks and well-telegraphed talking points , the message was that old-line Democrats in the House had failed to embrace the New Democrat moderate mandate of 1992. The “triangulation” strategy of the next year was as much about steamrolling old-school progressives as it was about winning over moderates.

But sometimes, when things are particularly bad , the blame game happens before the loss. And for Republicans, this is definitely one of those times.

You can find lots of Republican lawmakers who will point out that the Trump administration’s policies — the circular war-not-a-war with Iran, the foreign beef imports, the trade war with Canada, aggressive immigration raids, etc. — are not helping the party look its best to swing voters this year. This is gentle stuff, often attached to a reedy wish that, any day now, the ship of state will turn to fairer seas. And almost never is it phrased as a direct criticism of the president himself.

President Trump , you will not be surprised to hear, is being neither gentle nor indirect with his party.

The president’s main PAC has been piling up cash like crazy but only last week tapped into its more than $400 million war chest to help a candidate. But it was not tapped to beat a Democrat. Instead it was a rescue package for Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) to defeat her fellow Republican Rep. Ralph Norman (S.C.) in this week’s Senate primary runoff. This is in a state where Democrats haven’t gotten within 10 points of winning a Senate seat for decades.

Those Republicans grousing about the fact that the president hasn’t ponied up to try to save as many GOP seats as he can should remember that while Trump has a mixed record against Democrats — two presidential wins, one presidential loss and a 2018 midterm walloping — he is the greatest in the world at beating Republicans. Fighting his adopted party is what Trump does best.

In the wintertime, back when Republicans still believed that a combination of a strong economy and mid-decade gerrymandering would certainly save the Senate and might keep the House on-side, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles promised that the president was going to campaign for his party’s candidates “like it’s 2024 again.” The strategy was to deploy the president to motivate low-propensity MAGA voters who voted for Trump three times but aren’t moved to help the president’s party. It was a bold but not crazy strategy, at least not at the time before Trump’s job approval hit the skids post-Iran.

What is clear, though, is that Trump really agrees with those low-propensity voters. He likes himself, but doesn’t much care for the GOP.

This week, the president dredged up a 2025 social media post from one of his supporters excoriating Republicans for not doing more to support the Trump agenda. That will sound strange to most Americans who mostly see the Republican Party as an extension of Trump himself. But the argument goes that by refusing to do things like abolishing the Senate filibuster to jam through major legislation or by negotiating with Democrats over immigration enforcement funding, it’s actually congressional Republicans who are the problem.

This is a steroidal version of the argument that Obama and Clinton made in their times that voters are punishing recalcitrance. The difference, other than the f-bombs, is that Trump is doing it now instead of the second week of November.

Of course, what vulnerable Republicans need most of all right now is distance from an unpopular president. Democrats are massively motivated and core Republican voters are dispirited not because of Senate procedural rules but because of Iran and high prices. To survive in swing states and districts, Republicans need room to maneuver and, most of all, to get Trump off the front page for a while instead of, you know, renaming parts of the Great Lakes .

If endangered Republicans don’t like that, they’d better strap in, because it only gets worse from here. The Atlantic got a look at the strategy for how Trump plans to spend whatever funds he will share from his MAGA war chest. He’s going with more cowbell: huge ad buys praising himself for his accomplishments. It’s a very Trumpy answer, but maybe one with some advantages. If there really are dispirited hardcore MAGA voters, perhaps being reminded of the good old days of 2024 will lighten the mood and get them voting.

Will that be worth the downside of putting Trump in swing voters’ living rooms even more than he already is? Unlikely.

Republicans will gather in Dallas next month for the party’s first-ever midterm convention, which sounds like it’s going to be a two-day infomercial for MAGA: Democrats are communists so come join us in the new Golden Age. One suspects that it will be a lot of preaching to the choir as the congregation heads for the aisles.

Harper’s Magazine : “On August 5, 2013, a man and a woman ate a burger. Not just any burger: a world-historical burger, made from cattle cells grown in a lab by Mark Post , a professor of vascular physiology at Maastricht University in the Netherlands. The burger had taken two years to produce and cost $330,000, money furnished by the Google co-founder Sergey Brin . Now it was being tasted in public for the first time at Riverside Studios in London, at an event attended by two hundred members of the press and livestreamed to thousands. … The event—the theatrical reveal, the PR spectacle—triggered a kind of gold rush. One hundred and forty companies sprang up in six continents, trying to replicate what Post had done with beef across a range of other species: chicken, pork, fish, even quail. Investment to the tune of $3 billion flooded into the sector. … And yet, despite the frenzy, the meat itself never arrived.”

PRIME CUTS: THE COURTS WEIGH IN, MONEY ISSUES ENSUE AND SENATE HOPEFULS CHANGE KEY

Judge halts Ohio proof-of-citizenship requirement for voters and drivers: The Washington Post : “A federal judge temporarily blocked Ohio from requiring proof of citizenship when registering to vote at motor vehicle offices, a setback for conservative efforts to tighten voter registration rules ahead of the November midterms. Ohio’s law requiring proof of citizenship at Bureau of Motor Vehicles’ offices conflicts with the federal National Voter Registration Act, the court said. A preliminary injunction was granted on Tuesday. The Ohio rules were challenged by Red Wine & Blue, a liberal activist group centered on suburban women, and the Ohio Alliance for Retired Americans. President Donald Trump has tried unsuccessfully to impose national rules requiring voters to show proof of citizenship, although there is little evidence of widespread noncitizen voting.”

Massachusetts judge challenges Trump’s mail-in voting crackdown: Axios : “A Massachusetts judge ruled Tuesday that the Trump administration violated a nationwide injunction by finalizing a rule that would significantly overhaul mail voting if allowed to take effect. The order allows the Trump administration to publish the rule Wednesday, but the U.S. Postal Service remains barred from making the dramatic changes to mail-in ballots. ‘Defendants cannot contend that they misunderstood the scope of the court’s order,’ U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani wrote in a five-page filing Tuesday afternoon. ‘Accordingly, despite the Defendants’ protestations that “[t]he United States takes its obligation to comply with court orders very seriously,” the court finds that Defendants violated the preliminary injunction in this case.’ … The Trump administration argued in an Aug. 25 filing that publishing the new rule did not violate the nationwide injunction because the rule’s language specifically says the USPS won’t implement the rule while the injunction is in place. Therefore, merely publishing the rule doesn’t violate Talwani’s order.”

A potential court ruling could help Dems out in their cash issue: Semafor : “Democrats got some good news when the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that political parties and joint fundraising committees do not qualify for the candidate rate for political spending, which is lower than what outside groups have to pay. If the ruling stands — still a big ‘if’ — it would benefit Democrats. Democratic candidates are often outraising Republicans in key races, and those candidates would receive more efficient ad spending rates than political parties. Republicans will appeal to the Supreme Court; National Republican Senatorial Committee spokesperson Joanna Rodriguez said, ‘This is the first word, not the last.’ But Democrats are celebrating the decision, which blunts some of the Supreme Court’s ruling earlier this year allowing more coordinated spending between parties and candidates.”

Michigan GOP Senate campaign tells AIPAC to back off: Axios : “Allies of Mike Rogers , Michigan’s GOP nominee for the U.S. Senate, have asked AIPAC [American Israel Public Affairs Committee] not to advertise on his behalf, triggering a rupture with the powerful but polarizing pro-Israel group. Rogers spoke with AIPAC chair Michael Tuchin in Los Angeles last week. The next day, AIPAC shelved an already-cut video ad targeting Rogers’ Democratic rival, outspoken Israel critic Abdul El-Sayed . The extraordinary tension underscores how far AIPAC’s political standing has fallen amid voters’ anger over the war in Gaza. Even Rogers — a staunchly pro-Israel Republican — fears the group’s public support could be a liability in the Nov. 3 election. The move by Rogers’ team angered AIPAC officials, who had spent more than $30 million to try to defeat El-Sayed in the Democratic primary and prepared to spend millions more to help elect Rogers, according to people familiar with the conversations. El-Sayed made AIPAC a centerpiece of his successful primary campaign, using the group’s spending against him to portray Democratic opponent Haley Stevens as beholden to the pro-Israel lobby.”

Iowa poll shows GOP ahead for Senate, behind for governor: The Hill : “The Democratic and Republican candidates in the Iowa Senate and gubernatorial races are locked in tight battles, a new survey shows. The poll, which Suffolk University in Boston conducted Aug. 20-23, found that 45 percent of 500 respondents backed GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson in the Iowa Senate race, while 41 percent supported Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek . In the governor’s race, state Auditor Rob Sand (D) leads with 48 percent support over Republican businessman Zach Lahn ’s 44 percent. Lahn has never held elected office. The advantages for Hinson and Sand were within the margin of error of 4.4 percentage points.”

Turek to Kamala: Thanks, but no thanks: The Hill : “Iowa Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek on Wednesday shot down the idea of former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigning for him. When pressed by a reporter at a Wednesday event in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, about the topic of working with Harris during his campaign, Turek — a state representative and two-time Paralympic basketball gold medalist with a history of winning in conservative areas — simply responded, ‘No.’ Turek, who clinched his Senate nomination in early June, is the latest to join other red-state candidates who have attempted to distance themselves from the former vice president. His fellow Iowa Democrat, gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand, also pushed back against the idea of Harris campaigning for him — adding that he believes she shouldn’t pursue a presidential run in 2028.”

Paxton trails for Senate as the rest of Texas GOP surges ahead: Texas Public Opinion Research : “The poll finds Democrat James Talarico (48%) leading Republican Ken Paxton (42%) by six points in the U.S. Senate race. Meanwhile, Republican Greg Abbott (49%) leads Democrat Gina Hinojosa (42%) by seven points in the Governor’s race. In the Attorney General’s race, Republican Mayes Middleton leads Democrat Nathan Johnson by three points (44% to 41%).”

articles.title: Democratic senators demand Israeli government halt West Bank settlement expansion plans
articles.summary: A group of Democratic senators is calling on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to reverse a planned housing development in the West Bank that would effectively divide the Palestinian territory. In a Friday joint statement led by Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego (D), more than a dozen lawmakers expressed concerns over the government’s decision to open…
articles.body:
A group of Democratic senators is calling on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to reverse a planned housing development in the West Bank that would effectively divide the Palestinian territory.

In a Friday joint statement led by Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego (D), more than a dozen lawmakers expressed concerns over the government’s decision to open bidding last week on construction in the E1 area east of Jerusalem.

“The United States must remain committed to a two-state solution that delivers lasting peace and security for both the Jewish, democratic State of Israel and for a future Palestinian state,” the Democrats wrote in their statement. “Construction in E1 would take us further away from that goal.”

These expansion plans are set to occur in the West Bank’s E1 area and consist of seven residential compounds with a total of 1,234 housing units, according to The Times of Israel .

A tender published by Israel’s Construction and Housing Ministry on Aug. 18 gives contractors until a deadline of Oct. 19 to bid on the project.

The lawmakers warned the construction could isolate East Jerusalem from population centers like Bethlehem and Ramallah. The expansion project has been stalled for decades and faced ongoing backlash within the region and from abroad.

“For decades, Republican and Democratic administrations have recognized that development in E1 would seriously jeopardize the prospects for a Palestinian state,” the lawmakers wrote. “That concern remains just as urgent today.”

Twenty-nine Democrats signed on to the statement — Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (N.H.), Jeff Merkley (Ore.), Tim Kaine (Va.), Chris Coons (Del.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii), Cory Booker (N.J.), Chris Van Hollen (Md.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Patty Murray (Wash.), Chuck Schumer (N.Y.), Dick Durbin (Ill.), Jack Reed (R.I.), Amy Klobuchar (Minn.), Mark Warner (Va.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Ed Markey (Mass.), Tammy Baldwin (Wis.), Martin Heinrich (N.M.), Elizabeth Warren (Mass.), Gary Peters (Mich.), Catherine Cortez Masto (Nev.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Ben Ray Luján (N.M.), Alex Padilla (Calif.), Adam Schiff (Calif.), Lisa Blunt Rochester (Del.), Angela Alsobrooks (Md.), Elissa Slotkin (Mich.) and Peter Welch (Vt.).

The new congressional request cited a separate letter signed by 44 Democratic senators and independent Sen. Angus King (Maine) — who caucuses with the Democrats — on Wednesday, calling for the Israeli government to take immediate action against reported violence from Israeli settlers toward Palestinians in the West Bank.

“We urge the Israeli government to immediately rescind these tenders, halt settlement expansion in the West Bank, and take urgent action to rein in settler violence,” the Democrats wrote in their Friday statement.

“Without a change in course, Israel risks weakening its international standing and undermining its prospects for long-term security,” they continued. “We also urge the Trump administration to make full use of its existing authorities, including targeted sanctions on individuals and entities.”

President Trump has historically enjoyed a close relationship with the Israeli leader and defended him against criticism from U.S. lawmakers, but tensions have emerged between the two heads of state amid the Iran war and the implementation of a Gaza peace plan.

Trump appeared to ramp up pressure on Netanyahu to accept the terms of the peace deal when he withheld his endorsement in the prime minister’s reelection race during a Fox News interview last week.

The Israeli leader has pushed back on the proposal, which would require his military to withdraw from Gaza. Netanyahu said the move would require the complete disarmament of the U.S.-designated terrorist group Hamas.

articles.title: Trump's pick for FDA faces scrutiny after cyclospora outbreak
articles.summary: Heidi Overton has been tapped to lead the Food and Drug Administration. But some worry she will pick loyalty to Trump over science.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's new choice to lead the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) faces a tough road ahead, after several foodborne illness outbreaks this summer left many Americans sick and frustrated with their government.

Trump has picked White House aide and doctor Heidi Overton to lead the agency. But former and current FDA officials fear the Trump ally will prioritise loyalty to the president over rebuilding an agency that has lost much of its leadership and many members of staff.

"She's taking over an agency where the morale is low," said John Swartzberg, a professor emeritus of infectious diseases UC Berkeley's School of Public Health. "This is going to be very difficult for her to improve."

She was nominated to the post after a particularly bad summer of foodborne illnesses. While such outbreaks occur each year, when warmer conditions fuel growth of bacteria, experts say the cyclospora infections have been unprecedented and health officials have seemed slower to identify contamination issues.

She must be confirmed to the post by the Senate. No date for her hearing has been set.

What to know about deadly 'explosive diarrhoea' outbreak in US

Using a bathroom 20 times a day - life in the middle of US cyclospora outbreak

Taco Bell removes lettuce from menu in US after links to explosive diarrhoea parasite

This summer, the US saw over 17,000 confirmed cases of explosive diarrhoea caused by cyclospora - linked to lettuce from Taylor Farms - up from 1,180 cases last summer. There have also been outbreaks of E. coli and salmonella from alfalfa sprouts, eggs, jalapenos, frozen blueberries and a number of other products.

The recalls have left Americans baffled about what is safe to consume, as public health experts say the slow response to the outbreaks is a symptom of a depleted FDA.

"People are definitely upset about the outbreaks this summer, and they have a reason to be," said Sarah Sorscher, a food safety advocate with nonprofit Center for Science in the Public Interest.

"This is already a system that was teetering on the brink, and the cuts from the past year and the disruptions from the past year are pushing it over the edge."

The Health and Human Services department contests this.

"The Trump Administration has mounted a robust response to each outbreak," a spokesperson said.

"FDA has the staff needed to continue investigating outbreaks, as no FDA investigators were affected by staffing changes or reductions in force."

'It puts the scare into you': A summer of food illnesses

While some Americans are willing to give Trump's new FDA leader a shot, others worry the Trump administration's policies at the FDA have put their health at risk this summer.

Texas resident David Hargrave is on edge after having had diarrhoea every single day for the past month and a half, since the 59-year-old contracted cyclospora around the Fourth of July.

"It puts the scare into you," Hargrave said about knowing what to eat.

Food regulation experts say that a major contributing factor in these outbreaks has been deep cuts at the FDA, which they say has led to fewer food inspections and poor communication about outbreaks.

"If we had had better boots on the ground in that [cyclospora] outbreak, we could have potentially solved it," Sorscher said.

In the case of cyclospora, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued its first health alert on 14 July, 10 weeks after the first cases began in early May.

"It's resulted in a public that's a little more on edge and panic about what's going on because of the poor communication," said Jerold Mande, a former FDA and USDA official and a professor of nutrition at Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health.

Toby Davis got the parasite too after eating at Taco Bell, sending him to the emergency room.

Davis said he knows foodborne outbreaks happen every summer, but he believes the firings of agency workers with years of expertise slowed down the response to the parasite that sickened him and thousands of others.

"This is the result of those bad mistakes," the independent voter said. " Do I believe we'll contract more things from their negligence? Absolutely."

Even some supporters of the current health agenda are wary about whether the Trump administration cuts were helpful. Jacqueline Capriotti, who identifies with the "Make America Healthy Again" (MAHA) movement started by Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, said food safety must be a priority for the FDA.

"We're encouraging - 'eat real food' - well we have to make sure that that food is safe," Capriotti said, referencing Kennedy's nutritional message to Americans.

The FDA has been without a commissioner for nearly 3.5 months, after former leader Marty Makary resigned over a reported clash with the White House. Makary had reportedly refused to support Trump's plan to lift a ban on flavoured vapes, over concern it would encourage addiction amongst youths. Soon after his exit, several senior leaders also left the agency.

The wave of departures follows deep staffing cuts the previous year, when Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy fired 20% of employees at the FDA as part of the administration's widespread efforts to slash the civil service.

For years, many food scientists and health activists have tried to argue for more FDA funding, not less. And the cuts and leadership uncertainty have not helped fuel trust in the organisation that is in charge of regulating 80% of America's food supply.

Trump has praised Overton, a former general surgery resident at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and chief policy officer at conservative think tank America First Policy Institute, as a "rockstar" future leader of the FDA.

But her nomination to the top job comes at a time where Trump officials are attempting to take steps on a number of controversial issues regulated by the agency, including vaccines and abortion medication.

As an insider in Trump's orbit, some public health experts, including Swartzberg, are afraid she will put his agenda first, and the science second.

In a statement to the BBC, White House spokesperson Kush Desai said Overton “has been integral to ensuring that the Administration's policies are correct, consistent, and grounded in Gold Standard Science.

"The White House looks forward to her swift confirmation by the Senate."

But to be confirmed, Overton must first get the support of the Senate's health committee, chaired by Republican Senator and doctor Bill Cassidy. It's unclear whether Cassidy will back the president's pick, after he expressed "strong concerns" about Overton because of her support for Trump's orders to overhaul the childhood vaccine schedule.

Her nomination is also viewed sceptically by some in MAHA movement, because of Trump's order to increase domestic production of glyphosate, which they argue causes cancer.

One prominent MAHA influencer, Alex Clark, took to social media last week to accuse Overton of being heavily involved in the executive order, an allegation the White House denies.

Yet Capriotti said some in the movement were too quick to raise concerns.

"She's a well-respected doctor," Capriotti said. "I would like to give her a chance."
